promptText: Why is horizontal scaling generally preferred over vertical scaling for an AI-augmented web service?
options: Vertical scaling is always cheaper per unit of compute than horizontal scaling

Horizontal scaling adds many stateless instances behind a load balancer, avoiding the single-machine ceiling and single point of failure that vertical scaling eventually hits, and elastically absorbs unpredictable, high-latency AI traffic better than one larger machine
Vertical scaling cannot run any GPU-backed workload under any circumstance
Horizontal scaling eliminates the need for a load balancer entirely
explanation: Vertical scaling hits a physical ceiling and remains a single point of failure; horizontal scaling requires statelessness but scales further and adds redundancy, which suits AI workloads whose request volume is unpredictable and per-request latency is high.

promptText: Why can't a team simply add more of its own application servers to get past a model provider's rate limit?
options: The provider's tokens-per-minute or requests-per-minute quota is enforced against the account/API key at the provider, not per server, so more application servers just generate more requests funneling into the same shared, metered ceiling
Adding more servers is technically impossible for any cloud-hosted application
Provider rate limits automatically increase whenever a company's server count increases
Rate limits only apply to the first server that connects to the provider
explanation: A provider's quota is metered against the API key/account, independent of how many of your own servers issue requests, so more servers alone only produces more requests competing for the same fixed external ceiling.

promptText: Why can a 'cold start' for an LLM inference server take far longer than a typical application's cold start?
options: LLM servers always run on slower CPUs than typical applications

Beyond runtime startup, an LLM cold start also involves loading multi-gigabyte model weights into GPU memory and initializing the serving engine's internal state (KV-cache allocators, compiled kernels), steps a typical stateless service never has to perform
LLM cold starts are actually faster than typical application cold starts in every case
Cold start time for an LLM server is determined entirely by network latency to the client
explanation: A typical service's cold start is mostly runtime startup; an LLM server's cold start additionally requires pulling/loading large weights into GPU memory and warming up serving-engine internals, which can dominate total startup time.

promptText: Why is true 'scale-to-zero' harder to achieve well for GPU-backed inference than for stateless web services?
options: GPUs cannot be turned off once started

Loading model weights onto a GPU and initializing CUDA context can take tens of seconds to minutes, so the first request after idling pays a large latency penalty that is often unacceptable for interactive traffic, unlike a web container that starts in seconds
Scale-to-zero is only a concept that applies to databases, never to compute
GPU nodes are always billed at a flat monthly rate regardless of usage, making scale-to-zero pointless
explanation: A plain container can start in seconds, but a GPU model server's cold start (weight loading, CUDA initialization, kernel warm-up) is much longer, so teams often keep a small always-warm floor instead of true zero to protect interactive latency.

promptText: Why does an LLM-backed service need backpressure more urgently than a typical CRUD service?
options: CRUD services never experience traffic spikes

A typical CRUD request completes in milliseconds so bursts clear quickly, but an LLM call can take seconds, so unmanaged incoming traffic accumulates into a large number of concurrently in-flight, slow requests very fast, exhausting connections and memory
Backpressure is only relevant for batch processing pipelines, not real-time services
LLM services are always over-provisioned, so backpressure is never actually needed
explanation: Because LLM calls have much higher latency than typical CRUD operations, by Little's Law the same arrival rate produces far more concurrently in-flight requests, making backpressure (bounded queues, shedding, retry-after signals) essential to avoid collapse.

promptText: How can a thundering herd occur in an LLM-backed service even without any change in overall traffic pattern?
options: A popular cached response expires, and every concurrent request for that same prompt simultaneously misses the cache and hits the expensive provider call at once, spiking load and cost momentarily
Thundering herd can only happen during a DDoS attack, never from normal cache behavior
Thundering herd occurs when a single user sends one request per minute
Thundering herd is exclusively a database replication phenomenon, unrelated to LLM caching
explanation: When a hot cache entry expires, all concurrent callers for that same query miss simultaneously and hit the origin at once; mitigations include request coalescing, staggered TTLs, and pre-emptive refresh before expiry.

promptText: Using Little's Law (L = lambda x W), why must an LLM-backed service's capacity be planned around the number of concurrent in-flight requests (L) rather than just the arrival rate (lambda) alone?
options: Because L is always numerically smaller than lambda, so it under-states required capacity

Because average request duration (W) is much larger for LLM calls than for typical requests, so the same arrival rate produces a surprisingly large number of simultaneously in-flight requests that determine actual connection, thread, and memory needs
Because Little's Law only applies to systems with exactly one server
Because lambda is measured in tokens while L is measured in requests, making them impossible to compare
explanation: Since W (time in system) is much larger for LLM calls, the same request rate yields more concurrent in-flight work than a low-latency CRUD system would; sizing for L, not just raw requests-per-second, avoids undersizing connection pools and memory.

promptText: How does continuous batching improve GPU utilization compared to static batching for LLM inference?
options: Continuous batching processes only one request at a time, avoiding contention entirely

Static batching waits for a fixed batch to fully finish before starting a new one, wasting GPU cycles on sequences that finish early but must wait for stragglers; continuous batching admits new requests into a running batch the instant a slot frees up, keeping the GPU continuously fed
Continuous batching eliminates the need for a GPU altogether by running purely on CPU
Static batching and continuous batching produce identical GPU utilization; the only difference is API syntax
explanation: Static, fixed-size batches force early-finishing sequences to idle until the whole batch completes; continuous batching immediately backfills freed slots with new requests, which is why modern high-throughput inference engines outperform naive fixed-batch serving on variable-length generation.

promptText: Why is CPU utilization often a poor autoscaling signal for a Spring Boot service that mainly orchestrates LLM calls?
options: CPU utilization is not a metric Kubernetes is capable of measuring

The service spends most of its time waiting on network I/O for a slow model provider response rather than doing CPU-bound work, so CPU can stay low even while queue depth and latency climb sharply under load
CPU-based autoscaling is banned by most cloud providers for AI workloads
CPU utilization only matters for GPU nodes, never for orchestration-tier CPU-only pods
explanation: An I/O-bound orchestration workload can look comfortably idle on CPU while the real bottleneck (waiting on the provider) drives up latency and queue depth, so signals like in-flight request count or queue depth track the true bottleneck better.

promptText: A provider enforces both a requests-per-minute (RPM) limit and a tokens-per-minute (TPM) limit. Given average tokens per request, how is the effective maximum sustainable request rate determined?
options: It always equals the RPM limit, since RPM is the only binding constraint that ever matters

It is the minimum of the RPM limit and (TPM limit divided by average tokens per request), whichever binds first — meaning reducing average tokens per request directly raises the achievable request-rate ceiling under a fixed TPM quota
It is the sum of RPM and TPM limits combined into one number
TPM limits are advisory only and never actually throttle traffic
explanation: The effective ceiling is whichever quota binds first; because TPM divided by tokens-per-request can be the tighter constraint, shrinking average tokens per request (shorter prompts, capped output) is a legitimate scaling lever, not merely a cost lever.

promptText: Why must rate limiting for a horizontally scaled AI service be implemented as a distributed, shared-state mechanism rather than a local, per-pod, in-memory limiter?
options: Per-pod limiters are always slower to evaluate than distributed ones

A local limiter on each pod cannot see what every other pod is consuming, so the fleet can collectively overshoot the provider's true aggregate ceiling even though each individual pod believes it is within its own limit
Distributed rate limiters are required by law for any API integration
Local rate limiters cannot be implemented in Java at all
explanation: Because the provider's quota applies to aggregate consumption across the whole fleet, only a shared view (e.g., a Redis-backed limiter) can accurately reflect and enforce that ceiling; independent per-pod limiters can each look compliant while collectively exceeding it.

promptText: Why is a dead letter queue (DLQ) useful in an asynchronous LLM pipeline such as a batch document-embedding job queue?
options: A DLQ makes every message process successfully on the first attempt

It isolates messages that repeatedly fail permanently (malformed input, oversized documents, persistent provider errors) so they don't block the queue with endless retries or get silently dropped, keeping the main pipeline's throughput unaffected
A DLQ replaces the need for any retry logic in the pipeline
A DLQ is only relevant to synchronous, request/response APIs, not queues
explanation: Without a DLQ, permanently failing messages either retry forever (consuming worker capacity) or vanish silently; routing them to a DLQ preserves them for later inspection while keeping healthy traffic flowing at full throughput.

promptText: Designing traffic shaping for a Spring AI chat service that must stay under a strict provider tokens-per-minute ceiling during a viral spike, which layering order is correct and why?
options: Cache first (removes repeat traffic from the token budget entirely), then a distributed rate limiter with internal headroom and request prioritization, then an LLM gateway with key pooling/fallback to multiply effective quota, then circuit breakers/bulkheads to contain remaining failures, then graceful degradation as the last resort
Apply circuit breakers first, then disable caching to guarantee fresh answers, then rate limit only after the provider has already returned 429s
Route everything to the flagship model first since it has its own separate unlimited quota, then apply caching only if that fails
Skip rate limiting entirely and rely solely on the provider's own throttling to shed excess load
explanation: Cache first because it is free capacity removed from the quota entirely, rate limiting second to prevent self-inflicted overshoot with a global (not per-pod) limiter, gateway/fallback third to multiply effective quota across keys/providers, and resilience/degradation last to contain the blast radius of whatever still exceeds capacity.

promptText: Latency to an LLM provider spikes badly under load even though CPU, memory, and the provider's own status page look healthy. What is the most likely root cause to investigate first, and why does it masquerade as provider slowness?
options: The provider is definitely lying about its status page, so escalate directly to their support team

HTTP client connection pool exhaustion (undersized max connections in WebClient/RestClient) — additional requests queue waiting to acquire a pooled connection, and that queuing delay is indistinguishable from provider slowness unless pool acquisition time is specifically instrumented
The JVM garbage collector must be paused indefinitely, which is unrelated to connection handling
DNS resolution failures are the only possible cause of latency that doesn't show up in CPU or memory metrics
explanation: An undersized connection pool silently serializes requests that should run in parallel; the resulting queuing delay looks identical to provider slowness from the outside unless pool acquisition metrics (active/pending/idle connections) are checked directly.

promptText: How should a team decide, architecturally, between adding more hosted-provider capacity/API keys versus moving to self-hosted inference as an AI product grows?
options: Always self-host as soon as any rate limit is ever hit, regardless of traffic volume or predictability

Treat it as a build-versus-buy tradeoff hinging on sustained volume and predictability: bursty or moderate traffic usually favors staying hosted with strong traffic-shaping engineering, while consistently high, predictable volume favors self-hosting to remove the external quota ceiling and lower marginal cost — often as a hybrid rather than all-or-nothing
Always stay hosted forever, since self-hosting is never economically justified at any scale
The decision should be based solely on which option has the simpler README documentation
explanation: Hosted providers offer elastic capacity with no operational burden but bound you to their quotas and pricing; self-hosting removes the external ceiling in exchange for owning GPU capacity and serving infrastructure, so the right call depends on sustained volume and predictability, often resolving into a hybrid baseline-plus-burst approach.
